title: Exodus, looking back
hookLine: a bush, a sea, manna, a mountain
tomorrow: is there a prayer for feeling two things at once?

lines: ONE BOX SAYS DO NOT LOSE.
cards: Moving day has its own logic. Most boxes say kitchen or books, and one says do not lose. On the night Israel leaves Egypt, in a hurry, with bread that had no time to rise, Exodus stops for one detail.
Moses is carrying something that isn't food or gold. It belongs to a man who died long before.

teach.h: MOSES TOOK THE BONES OF JOSEPH.
teach.b: “And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him.” Joseph had made his family swear it: when God brings you out, carry my bones up from here.
So the road out of slavery begins with a promise kept to the man from yesterday's story. Exodus, looking back, is that road.
A shepherd sees a bush on fire and not burning up, and says, “I will now turn aside, and see this great sight.” Only when he turns does a voice call his name. The sea opens.

teach.h: MANNA: THEY WIST NOT WHAT IT WAS.
teach.b: In the wilderness something lies on the ground each morning, and the people say, “It is manna: for they wist not what it was.” Wist means knew. They ate a question, and there was enough for each day.
Then the mountain, and words that begin by remembering: “I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.”

This story belongs first to the Jewish people, and Christians read it too; in the Gospels, Jesus's last supper falls at Passover. Here's the detail to tell a friend: the road to freedom carries a coffin.

how: Christians read Exodus in worship and study, and some churches read its story of the sea crossing during the Easter season.

games.q: your cousin is moving abroad for work and feels guilty, as if leaving means betraying the family. which Exodus detail fits best?
o: Moses carried Joseph's bones: you can leave and still carry who you come from.
a real exodus means cutting every tie with the old place.
staying put is always the more faithful choice.
games.why: the road out of Egypt began with a promise kept: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write two short lines. First, one thing you're leaving, or hope to leave: a habit, a fear, a place. Second, one thing you'll carry with you when you go, the way Moses carried Joseph's bones.
If you pray, offer both lines to God.
